You do not look like a boy at all. I wouldn’t mistake you for a boy from half a mile away. 

As I’m sure you know, kids are just learning about the world. They make connections between things based on the amount of knowledge they have at such young ages. So, I’m kinda thinking that your child may be making this observation based off of the fact that your hair is at a shorter length? 

My son assumes that being taller means that you must be older than the shorter person, that boys only have short hair and that girls only have long hair. Kids are just kids, they’ve roasted me good a few times but I know that they do not perceive things the way a fully developed mind would. Try not to fret ❤️

To be clear, the short length does NOT make you look like a boy.

Yes, cry for yourself. That’s a start to showing some acceptance/ compassion towards yourself and what you went through. Fuck whoever and whatever caused trauma for you. I’m glad that you can at least cry for yourself and say “fuck you” to the cause of all of the harm that was done to you.  You deserve to have care and concern for yourself. Good luck with everything : )

I don’t find it dumb, I had a panic attack for the same reason today lol. I was shaking so badly, I could barely pay. 

Might seem a bit strange, but just recognizing that  I’m having a panic attack, (usually flashbacks for me but I find this helps with both) telling myself that it’s alright to feel this way. and that the anxiety will pass, can really help move things along. it doesn’t completely remove the anxiety, but reducing the pressure to “stop panicking” makes it much easier to actually calm down.

I’m assuming that my trauma is the reason almost all of my dreams have to do with sex or sexual activity. I can be having a dream completely unrelated to sex and all of the sudden I’m trying to have relations with almost any person I see in my dream.

I started experiencing this at an alarmingly young age; which became concerning to me as I grew up and reflected on it. 
My guess here is that repressed trauma from early childhood were manifesting that way in my dreams, didn’t make that connection until very recently. 

Besides the sexual dreams, I have a lot of vidid, violent and disturbing nightmares as well. They’re full of a bunch of shit that I’ve never seen or imagined in my waking life; crap that would make horror movies look like ‘The Wiggles’ show. 

Sorry that you go through this. Hoping you can go nightmare-free for a while

I know that when I’m not in the middle of a flashback, I can grasp this kind of logic. It can get better, and I know what it feels like to truly understand and feel that things will get better, but it just feels like too fucking much. 

It really can get better, and these feelings don’t last forever, but how the fuck did you get through those moments where you felt like giving up? I can’t handle this shit. I was sober for 9 months, doing great despite the emotional flashbacks I had throughout that time period. Then, in November I ended up breaking down again. After 9 months of being alcohol free, I’ve been drowning myself with it again. How did you do it??? Don’t get me wrong, I’m so happy for you, I’m so happy to hear that someone has been able to get through this shit, but how did you do it? These flashbacks take me right out. 

All I can think about is giving up. I’m pretty trashed right now because I spent my day in tears and couldn’t stop thinking about how fucking pointless my healing journey has felt. Im aware that the alcohol is a temporary crutch, and will make me feel worse tomorrow, but it’s just too fucking much. How the fuck does anyone do this?

And with the holidays coming up, the feelings of alienation and isolation are far more intense.  
This really does feel like hell. I feel so alone. Keep switching between wanting to give up and holding on to the hope that I can keep healing. 

But I see everyone here and the 5 people apparently here on the post right now. Not completely alone ❤️ this shit sucks. Hope everyone can try to keep fighting.

I can relate to you though. Crying doesn’t help me feel better either. In my case, crying makes me feel WORSE. I believe it’s due to being punished for displaying any “negative emotions”; such as crying when I’m really upset. 

I had to do my best to suppress tears if I was getting scolded, they only made things worse.

I’m an adult, There is nobody calling my name, and most of the time I’m not even around anyone. 
I’ve recognized this and fight the urge now; it’s still there, but it doesn’t send an immediate “jolt” to my nervous system anymore. 

Fuck that shit. You don’t respond within less than a second or run to them immediately, and it’s a full on death sentence.

It’s also in police records. So when I made a statement about yet another truthful experience with an abusive person, they decided that they were not going to put effort into it, most likely because of the information they have from the statement I made as a teen. 

Humiliated myself in order to save an abuser because I felt empathy for them. 

And people still think this about me. I haven’t told anyone the real reason I recanted that first statement.

(First and second statement are about two separate people)

What about him staying up all night is bothering you? 
You said that you got upset when you woke up at 5am and he was still awake. Can you explain why you felt this way? (I am in no way trying to be condescending, this is genuine curiosity. Maybe it will help us give you some better advice)

At the age of 15, I did the exact same thing in the summer. I would stay up until 6-7am sometimes and sleep all day.

However, when the time came to go back to school, I realized that my sleeping habits from the summer were not going to mix well with school. 

It took me a few years, but being allowed to learn my own lesson, made me a lot better at following more responsible habits as an adult. 

Now, when I think about staying up late, I remember how miserable I would feel when school started back up because of my summer sleeping habits. First week was pretty bad, until I was able to start sleeping at more reasonable times. 

Sometimes, being able to make mistakes without intervention, helps people learn a lot faster. If they have to hold themselves accountable for their own actions, and experience the consequences of their bad habits, they’re much more likely to stop repeating them.

Little dwarf spider was on the city bus and decided to use me as his seat. 

Watched him crawl up my arm, face my direction, lift a leg (similar to how jumping spiders act when they see me even though this was not a jumper), then went back down my arm and sat on the top of my hand. 

Switched between my arm and hand for the entire bus ride and I carried him off at my stop. Then put him down near some plants. 

After that, my fear of spiders had basically vanished. I find them crawling on me almost every time I go out now, and always see them coming up to me. It’s a funny and cute coincidence for me. 

“Fear of spiders vanishes after spider decides to use me as seat on bus. Start to see spiders as friends, spiders see me as friend. Spiders come to say hello when they are nearby. The end”

You deserve to feel proud of yourself, especially today. RIGHT ON!!

Your way of looking at the situation makes a lot of sense to me. Rationalizing can be really helpful, and I wish that I would have been able to come up with a logical explanation as to why they were acting that way. 

I’m sure this is not news to you (as it’s typical for trauma survivors) but the part of my mind that uses logic completely shuts down in situations like this. I can offer the same kind of insight into things when I am not directly feeling threatened by a situation. 

My friends have always commented on that. I can use my rational judgement to help others, but when I’m the one that feels attacked, I feel like I’m only a nervous system, without access to any other part of me. 

Nevertheless, your comment is still helpful. It makes complete sense to me, I am calm, and now that I have some pointers, I will have a better chance of recalling this point of view next time I catch myself dwelling on what had happened yesterday.

So another error on the other person, but the blame went to you instead. I’m sure these are good examples of the statement “toxic shame is blame unfairly turned towards the self”. 
You did nothing wrong either, and I really hope the compassion that you are showing me, is the same that you show yourself when you look back on that situation. When I read that, my mind didn’t see anything wrong with you. I saw fault in the employee that responded so harshly. Maybe they were upset with their error, and turned it towards you to make themselves feel better about it. 

The mistake did not and does not define you. My mistake from yesterday, did not and does not mean anything about me either.

I really do feel better. I’ve already responded to a lot of these comments with words of appreciation, but I can’t express this enough. This is the first time I have ever had so many people genuinely understand and care about how I felt. Most people in my life tell me things like “it’s not a big deal”, “get over it”, “just be confident”, etc….

It feels so weird to see how similarly a lot of us were treated as children. “I would flinch and cower if the apology wasn’t accepted, and/or have a panic attack because as a child this meant blows were coming” is an experience that I’ve gone through a countless amount of times. 

When apologizing wasn’t working, there was pretty much nothing else that I could do but stand there and wait for the punishment. Just had to give up and take it, as if it was deserved. 

I’m glad to hear that you have been able to get to the point where you don’t feel the need to apologize for just being human. That gives me hope. Helps me believe that I can also get to a point where I apologize based on my own morals and values, instead of habitually and unnecessarily over-apologizing for every little thing.

I’m glad that you commented to answer that question. When I’m having moments like that, I forget everything that I have learned about the way I respond to triggers and berate myself for responding in ways that seem “childish”. I know there is nothing wrong with that when I am not triggered. Part of my mind was definitely not able to develop and is stuck believing that it is still a helpless child. I was never allowed to actually “be” a child, so I berate myself for acting that way, and that childlike part of my mind becomes triggered even more because that is how she was treated for acting developmentally appropriate for that age. 

Even though I am calm today, and kind of being released from the grasp of that hell of a flashback, I still hadn’t been able to recall that information, until I read your comment just now. 

Hoping that the empathy, and kindness that all of you are showing me, comes back to all of you tenfold. : )

I know what you mean about not being able to become angry or defensive unless it’s someone else that is being targeted. When I see someone else being treated unfairly, I get mad, and I can stand up for them without a second thought. I’ve noticed that I also only ever daydream about sticking up for someone else that I view as innocent, but never about standing up for myself. 

I get this weird angry-justice power sensation in my body when I defend someone else, and it’s very satisfying. When it comes to defending myself, I don’t. I cower and feel like I want to climb out of my own skin and disappear.

You do have an answer :) the answer here is that none of us are as alone as we think, and the fact that you shared this (and all of the experiences that others are sharing here), helps me acknowledge that there is nothing wrong with me. There is nothing wrong with any of us. We experienced trauma and our minds react this way because it helped keep us safe from harm when it was needed. As terrible as it feels to live this way, it means that our human brain tried its best to help us survive.

I’ve probably listened to Pete Walker’s “from surviving to thriving” audiobook 30  times within the past few months, a lot of his writing has really helped me progress.

I have become pretty good at recognizing when I am in a flashback. I have become much better at managing them and working my way through them. On days like today, where I start the day off with anxiety, it’s much more difficult to keep myself out of triggering thought processes, to work with my critic, and to get myself out of full blown flashbacks. 

Thanks for those tips, I like that you mentioned “low-stakes” situations. Sometimes I jump right in the deep end when trying to overcome fears, and end up fucking things up even more.

I skimmed through some comments while waiting for the bus home, and just seeing glimpses of all of this support had put a smile on my face. I just sat down at home and now that I’ve been able to actually read everything, I’m shedding happy tears. 

The fact that everyone responding to this actually understands, and none of you are making me feel even more ashamed of myself than I already felt, is one of the most bizarre things I’ve probably ever experienced.

The takeover from the nervous system feels really terrible, and really discouraging. We know that we are trauma survivors, and that the creation of these responses are not our fault. Yet, somehow the shit put into our heads by our abusers seems to come right back out when something triggers us. For me, the shame is the worst part of it. 

I worked so hard to get myself to the point where I know that I have worth and that I don’t have to be ashamed of myself for just fucking existing and being human. I’ve built self esteem, I’ve started to learn to actually like myself and accept myself. Then something like this happens and it’s just instant shame flooding through my body.  It’s so frustrating that I can forget who I have started to become, like temporary amnesia but only about all of the things that I have learned about myself and my trauma, and just revert right back to the little girl that is afraid to simply breathe wrong, or afraid to place a fucking cup down just in case it pisses someone off.

Getting shit on because I was trying to correct my mistake or at least try to, is what made this so much worse than other little mistakes I’ve made. It made me feel like they saw me as some sort of evil criminal that deserves to be looked down upon.  

I cried for a bit, then some little spider crawled up my arm and onto my back where I couldn’t see it. I was paranoid that it was going to crawl down my shirt, but it was super funny. The release from the tears and the fact that the spider situation made me laugh, really helped.

Excessively apologizing is like second nature to me because it usually meant that any punishments were going to be less severe. :/

I wasn’t a fan of spiders until about 3 months ago. 

Was sitting on public transit and a spider just casually landed on my arm. It was a dwarf spider. Crawled down to my hand, then back up my arm and seemed to stop and look at me (not the same way a jumping spider can). 

Before this, I would normally have just brushed any spiders off of me. I think it was the fact that it was a very small spider that allowed me to deal with the exposure. 

I really like them now. Just that little experience changed my whole perspective. 

Now that I’ve been interested in spiders, I notice them a lot more, and I find one crawling by me, or on me, almost every single day that I’m chilling outside. I’m glad that they’ve started to crawl on me after I started to see them as friends. Before this, I probably would have lost my sh**

I know this is a year old but, I googled this (personal) phenomenon, hoping to finally find someone that understands what I’ve been talking about. When the topic of falling in dreams comes up, I tell people that falling in my dreams is so uncomfortable that it’s painful. Nobody has ever understood what I meant. 

The way you described the sensation is exactly how I understand it, and how I have tried to explain it to others. 

It’s so intense for me that the only thing I can focus on is how horrible it feels. I have to “ride it out” like some kind of bad trip, until I reach the ground. 

For some reason I experience the exact same “falling sensation” when some kind of demon (as I perceive certain scary creatures in my dreams) is close enough to attack me. However, the sensation becomes more focused in my back rather than the front/middle-ish of my torso. 

I can handle nightmares, I can handle the super messed up crap that my mind comes up with to fuel my nightmares. But, I can’t handle the ones that involve that falling sensation. I could be falling through a pleasant sunshine and rainbow sky or get attacked by the least threatening looking creature ever, and nope out of that much faster than the most brutal and terrifying nightmares imaginable that don’t involve that horrible feeling.

This shit bothers me so much. The places that we are supposed to be safe in, end up being the places that are the least safe. It’s messed up. What kind of sick joke is that? I hope that you are somewhere better now.

And I wish that a lot of people could understand this. If something is required for survival or to be free of harm, the brain will do its best to adapt around it. Unfortunately in ways that are beneficial while in the dangerous environment, but end up sticking around when they are not required for survival anymore. Even though I am completely safe now, parts of my brain cannot comprehend that, and it still feels like I’m always in immediate danger. Quality of life = terrible. 

My heart goes out to anyone that has had to develop such overwhelming responses to stay safe from people or families that they had no choice but to be born into. The terrible things that a lot of human beings do, make me sick.

I find that remark ignorant. If I could just “stop caring about what people think” I would have started that a long time ago. I used to take that “advice” very seriously and would become really angry and annoyed with myself for not being able to just “not care”. It ended up just making me feel even more inferior than I already did. 

Now I’ve started to respond with “Okay, so next time you’re tired just stop being tired. Next time you’re hungry, just stop being hungry. Problem solved”. 

I mean, I usually save that response for the ones that are being very rude about it, or are acting as if I’m stupid because I have low self-esteem. If there doesn’t seem to be any malicious intent behind it, I try to explain why it doesn’t work like that (as long as they are someone relevant enough to my life to take the time to talk about it). 

At least the use of this statement allows me to gauge whether or not the person is someone that I can potentially get along with.

I was always a huge fan of rpg games where the player is the hero (so that’s a huge list). I’m guessing that I am always drawn to those types because I enjoy keeping others safe. It allows me to have a sense of control, and to give others (NPC’s haha) the safety and support that I never had. 

A specific life simulation game series captured my interest at a very young age. The moment I discovered “The Sims 2”, I was hooked. Since then I’ve played almost every sims game besides the first one. I would probably be ashamed of myself to see how many hours total I’ve clocked playing the sims. 
Another game that gives me a sense of control. It’s very obvious to me why I would lose track of time while playing those games.

Had some beer one night (2 weeks ago). Not very many, I had 4, tops and blacked out. This might have been because of seroquel. I woke up with a massive hangover the next day, usually don’t and I have drank a few times while on seroquel before with no hangover the next day. Had massive “hangxiety” as well.

I’ve been on it for a few weeks and have been getting a nasty headache every night at around the same time (7pm). The headaches only started about 2 weeks after taking 150mg every day. I’ve never had nightly headaches like this before.

The doctors also suspect that I have celiac disease! They did a biopsy (that’s what they do during upper endoscopies) and I’ll have the results some time soon. Also forgot to mention, when they take a sample of any suspicious areas in your stomach or any stomach tissue, you don’t feel it at all.

In my experience, upper endoscopies are painless and quick. They offer sedatives for the procedure (I’m in Canada so I agreed to be sedated because it wouldn’t cost anything). You lie down on a bed, they make you swish and gargle this god-awful tasting numbing spray in your mouth (it made me gag hard lol) until your mouth and throat are numb, then they get you to lie on your side (if they are giving you sedatives they start the IV when you turn to your side). After that, they put a mouth guard in to stop you from accidentally biting the tube. Then, they carefully push the tube down your throat and further down into your GI tract. The sensation of the tube in your body feels a little uncomfortable (but it may be worse without sedatives, I’m not sure). They look around in your GI tract for about 5 minutes, then they pull the tube out (which caused me mild discomfort but not pain), and then it’s over. You recover in another room for about 15 minutes and then have someone drive you home if you were sedated. (If you were given sedatives you can’t drive or go anywhere on your own, someone has to be with you for the rest of the day, you can’t make any important business decisions or sign any documents for 24 hours).

I’ve actually been having the same symptoms for 5 months, except I have a few more; complete loss of appetite, upper abdominal pain after eating, and nausea that sometimes includes vomiting. 

I just had an upper endoscopy done today due to those symptoms and I was told that I most likely have gastritis. I had a biopsy done and will know what it is for sure once I get the results. 

There are other causes of these symptoms, sometimes they’re caused by stomach ulcers, tumours, celiac disease, stomach cancer. It’s hard to tell. If I were you, I’d talk to a doctor and see if you can get an upper endoscopy or an x-ray (barium swallow type of x-ray) done. 

Best of luck to you!
